unit_label: BFM Module D unit 5 (courseware unit 30): interest rate risk management

facts.statement: Introduction and essentials (courseware): until about 1970 regulatory restrictions meant deposits were taken at mandatory rates and lent at fixed rates, so interest rates were largely unaffected by market pressures; deregulation brought banks to the risk, and many bank failures in the 1970s to 1990s were triggered by poorly managed interest rate risk (long-term fixed rate assets funded by short-term volatile liabilities). In India, deregulation has given financial institutions operating freedom and the pricing of assets and liabilities is left to commercial judgement, so earnings and costs of liabilities are related to interest rate volatility and interest rate risk has become relevant. Interest rate risk is the exposure of the financial condition to adverse movements in interest rates; accepting the risk is a normal part of banking and an important source of profit, but excessive risk is a threat to earnings and capital. Changes in rates affect earnings by changing net interest income (NII) and other interest-sensitive income and operating expenses, and they affect the economic value of assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet instruments because the present value of future cash flows changes: rising rates raise the discount rate and reduce market values; mismatching maturities by holding longer-term assets than liabilities means that when rates rise the market value of assets falls by more than that of liabilities, exposing the bank to economic loss. Interest rate risk is volatility in NII or in net interest margin (NIM, NII divided by earning assets) due to changes in rates, arising from assets and liabilities with different principal amounts, maturity dates or repricing dates (rollover rates).

Gap or mismatch risk (courseware): a gap is the difference between assets and liabilities whose interest rates are reset during a given period; holding assets and liabilities with different principal amounts, maturity or repricing dates creates exposure to changes in rate levels. Example 1: a bank funds Rs 100 crore of two-year assets at 10 per cent with one-year liabilities at 9 per cent: the first-year profit spread is 1 per cent (Rs 1 crore); in the second year the liabilities must be rolled over, and if the rate on liabilities rises to 11 per cent the bank incurs a loss of 1 per cent (Rs 1 crore); a bank holding shorter-term assets than liabilities faces uncertainty about the rate at which it can reinvest. Example 2: a 91-day deposit at 8 per cent invested in a 91-day T-bill at 10 per cent has no mismatch and the 200 basis points spread is preserved. If the deposit funds a floating rate loan (repriced monthly at an initial 10 per cent), the bank is asset sensitive: the loan rate moves more rapidly than the deposit rate, so NII expands if rates rise and shrinks if rates fall. If a 91-day 8 per cent deposit funds a 5-year fixed rate mortgage loan at 10 per cent, the bank is liability sensitive: its deposit cost is reset more rapidly than the loan rate, so a rise in rates erodes NII and a fall expands it.

Basis risk (courseware): even in a perfectly matched gap position, the interest rates of two different instruments seldom change by the same degree during the same period; the risk that rates of different assets and liabilities change in different magnitudes is basis risk. Courseware example: repricing assets are call money 50 and cash credit 40 (total 90) against repricing liabilities savings deposit 50 and fixed deposits 50 (total 100): a negative gap of Rs 10 crore, so a 1 per cent parallel fall in rates should improve NII by Rs 1 crore. If instead call money falls 1.0 per cent, cash credit 0.7 per cent, savings deposits 0.5 per cent and fixed deposits 0.4 per cent: decrease in interest income = 0.50 + 0.28 = 0.78; decrease in interest expense = 0.25 + 0.20 = 0.45; loss in NII = 0.78 - 0.45 = Rs 0.33 crore. Basis risk is high for banks that create composite assets out of composite liabilities (the loan book funded by a composite liability portfolio) and in volatile rate scenarios.

Net interest position, embedded option, yield curve, price and reinvestment risks (courseware): net interest position risk arises when a bank earns interest on more assets than the liabilities on which it pays interest; a bank with a positive net interest position loses NII as rates fall and gains as they rise (it is exposed to the funding cost staying the same). Embedded option risk arises from prepayment of loans and bonds (with put or call options) and premature withdrawal of deposits before stated maturity: borrowers tend to pay off loans when rates fall, so the bank earns lower NII (courseware example: a 10 per cent 90-day loan funded by an 8 per cent 90-day certificate of deposit prepaid after 30 days when rates fall to 9 per cent: the bank earns 200 bp for 30 days and only 100 bp thereafter as it reinvests at 9 per cent). Yield curve risk: the yield curve plots yields of all maturities of an instrument; its slope and shape change over time and a change affects NII (courseware example: 3-year floating deposits and loans repriced quarterly, deposit rate 100 bp above the 91-day T-bill and loan rate 300 bp above the 364-day T-bill; with T-bills at 12.50 and 13 per cent the NII is 250 bp; if the curve inverts with 91-day at 14 per cent and 364-day at 13 per cent the NII falls to 100 bp). Price risk occurs when assets are sold before maturity: bond prices and yields are inversely related and the risk is associated with the trading book. Reinvestment risk is uncertainty about the rate at which future cash flows can be reinvested: the bond pricing formula assumes coupons are reinvested at the yield to maturity; if rates fall, the realised yield falls below the expected yield (courseware example: a bank with a zero coupon deposit promising to double in 7 years invests in a 7-year 12 per cent bond; if coupon reinvestment is only at 10 per cent after a year, it falls short). When rates rise the bond price falls (a capital loss) but reinvestment income rises, so price risk and reinvestment risk partly offset; short-term bonds have more reinvestment risk, long-term bonds more price risk; matching the duration of assets and liabilities (not their maturities) reduces reinvestment risk.

Effects: earnings and economic value perspectives (courseware): two complementary perspectives. Earnings perspective: the impact of rate changes on accrual or reported earnings, the traditional approach; the component with the most attention is net interest income; as banks expanded into fee-based activities, a broader focus on overall net income (interest and non-interest income and expenses) has become more common because non-interest income (loan servicing and securitisation fees, transaction processing fees) can also be rate sensitive (for example servicing fees based on the volume of mortgages fall when rates fall and mortgages prepay). Economic value perspective: the economic value of an instrument is the present value of its expected net cash flows discounted at market rates; the economic value of a bank is the present value of expected cash flows on assets minus the present value of expected cash flows on liabilities plus the present value of expected net cash flows on off-balance sheet positions; it shows the sensitivity of the net worth of the bank to rate changes and gives a more comprehensive view of the long-term effects than near-term earnings. Example: a 5-year 10 per cent government bond held by the bank with market rates rising to 12 per cent falls in price (a Rs 100 bond may fetch about Rs 95), a loss when marked to market. Embedded losses: instruments not marked to market may already contain gains or losses due to past rate movements that will be reflected over time in earnings (for example a long-term fixed rate loan entered into when rates were low and funded more recently at higher rates drains resources over its life).

Measurement techniques (courseware): a bank must identify and measure interest rate risk before managing it; measurement systems should assess all material sources of rate risk on assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet positions, use generally accepted financial concepts and techniques, and have well-documented assumptions and parameters. Techniques range from simple calculations to static simulation and dynamic modelling. Repricing schedules: the simplest technique distributes interest-sensitive assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet positions into time bands according to maturity (fixed rate) or time to next repricing (floating rate); items without definite repricing dates (sight deposits, savings accounts, mortgages with prepayment options) are assigned to bands by judgement and past experience. Gap analysis: the repricing gap in each band is rate sensitive assets less rate sensitive liabilities; multiplied by an assumed rate change it gives an approximation of the change in NII. A negative (liability sensitive) gap means that a rise in rates reduces NII; a positive (asset sensitive) gap means that a fall in rates reduces NII. Shortcomings: it ignores variation in characteristics within a band, differences in spreads between rates (basis risk), changes in the timing of payments, option-related positions, and non-interest income variability; it is only a rough approximation. Duration: sensitivity weights based on the duration of assets and liabilities in each band are applied to estimate the change in economic value from an assumed rate change; limitations: it focuses mainly on repricing risk, uses average duration per band, and the simplifying assumptions may not capture option risk. Simulation: static simulation assesses cash flows from current positions under rate scenarios (shifts or tilts of the yield curve) and discounts them to estimate the change in economic value; dynamic simulation adds assumptions about the future course of interest rates and expected changes in business activity (new loans, pricing strategy, behaviour of customers) and can capture the effect of embedded options, but should not become a black box. Difficult cases are positions where behavioural maturity differs from contractual maturity (mortgage prepayments and non-maturity deposits such as current and savings accounts), where banks use statistical analysis of past behaviour and prepayment models.

Strategies for controlling interest rate risk (courseware): the process begins with strategies that change the interest rate sensitivity of the balance sheet by altering components; some banks match assets and liabilities maturities as closely as possible to reduce the gap to zero and insulate NII; aggressive bankers vary the gap with their interest rate forecast (if they expect rates to rise, they widen the gap by repricing assets more frequently than liabilities). Reduce asset sensitivity: extend investment portfolio maturities, increase floating rate deposits, increase fixed rate lending, sell floating rate loans, increase short-term borrowings, increase long-term lending. Reduce liability sensitivity: reduce investment portfolio maturities, increase floating rate lending, increase long-term deposits, increase short-term lending. Other options: match long-term assets with non-interest-bearing liabilities, match repriceable assets with similar repriceable liabilities, use forward rate agreements, swaps, options and financial futures to construct synthetic securities and hedge exposure, and contain the volume of NPAs which accentuate maturity mismatch (large NPAs entail carrying non-interest earning assets funded by volatile liabilities). A full match is neither feasible nor prudent; risk-averse banks fix tolerance limits on rate sensitivity gaps, smaller for the shorter end or proximate time bands; the structure of all new debts is reviewed to protect margins; banks should develop in-house expertise to forecast rates.

Controls, supervision and sound practices (courseware): banks need adequate internal controls to ensure the integrity of the interest rate risk management process: a strong control environment and compliance culture, an adequate process for identifying and evaluating risk, control activities (policies, procedures, methodologies), adequate information systems and continual review of adherence; reviews should be done regularly by individuals independent of the function and, for complex exposures, by an independent party such as an internal or external auditor or risk management experts. Sound interest rate risk management has four elements: appropriate board and senior management oversight, adequate risk management policies and procedures, appropriate risk measurement, monitoring and control functions, and comprehensive internal controls and independent audits. The board of directors approves strategies and policies and is informed regularly of the exposure; senior management ensures the structure of the business and level of risk are effectively managed and maintains limits on risk taking, systems and standards for measuring risk, valuing positions and measuring performance, and a comprehensive reporting and review process; lines of responsibility and authority are clear, with separation of duties and independence of risk measurement, monitoring and control functions from position-taking functions.

Central bank guidelines on IRRBB (courseware, principles only): interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB) is the current or prospective risk to a bank capital and earnings arising from adverse movements in interest rates that affect banking book positions; changes in rates change the present value and timing of future cash flows, and affect earnings through net interest income. The existing guidelines on the ALM system bucket positions in time bands by rate sensitivity; for non-maturity deposits (current and savings deposits) banks estimate behavioural patterns and place them in appropriate buckets, those unable to do so use the standardised approach. Banks must compute capital for interest rate risk in trading book positions (added to risk-weighted assets) and under Pillar 2 identify the risks from changing rates on balance sheet and off-balance sheet exposures in the banking book from short-term and long-term perspectives; the central bank does not permit trading by banks in banking book securities. Enhanced guidelines (courseware): governance (a Board-approved risk appetite statement for IRRBB, regular monitoring of the nature and level of exposure, procedures to approve major hedging or risk-taking, systems to escalate violations of Board-approved limits, identification of IRRBB inherent in all products); measurement (compute IRRBB from earnings and economic value perspectives using internally selected shock scenarios, historical and hypothetical stress scenarios and prescribed scenarios). The dates, scenario counts and thresholds are not taught.

Supplementary material (courseware): interest rate sensitive gap = RSA - RSL; a positive gap (asset sensitive) has RSA > RSL, a negative gap (liability sensitive) RSA < RSL. Courseware table (Rs crore): 1 day: assets 500, liabilities 550, gap -50; >1 day to 3 months: 400 and 600, gap -200 (cumulative -250); >3 to 6 months: 700 and 800, -100 (-350); >6 to 12 months: 850 and 1050, -200 (-550); >12 months to 3 years: 1200 and 1500, -300 (-850); >3 to 5 years: 1500 and 1300, +200 (-650); >5 years: 2500 and 1850, +650 (0). The bank has a short-term negative gap and a long-term positive gap; with a cumulative one-year gap of Rs 550 crore, a 1 per cent rise in short-term rates reduces NII by Rs 5.50 crore. Risk and options: RSA - RSL > 0 (reinvestment risk): if rates fall NII falls as assets are reinvested at lower rates; options: extend assets maturity or shorten liability maturity. RSA - RSL < 0 (refinancing risk): losses if rates rise; options: shorten assets maturity or extend liability maturity. Modified duration gap method (steps): identify variables for each item, generate bucket-wise cash flows, determine the yield for each item, use the mid-point of each time bucket as the proxy maturity, calculate modified duration of each category, compute the weighted average modified duration of assets (DA) and liabilities (DL), and then DGAP = DA - W x DL where W = RSL / RSA. Modified duration of equity = DGAP x leverage, with leverage = RSA / equity (Tier 1 + Tier 2 capital). Illustration: net worth 1,350; RSA 18,251; RSL 18,590; DA 1.96; DL 1.25; W = 1.02; DGAP = 0.69; leverage 13.52; modified duration of equity 9.34; for a 200 basis point rate shock the fall in equity value is 18.68 per cent (9.34 x 2). Treatment of off-balance sheet items: foreign currency items converted at spot rates; interest rate swaps as a long and a short position in bonds (the fixed leg and floating leg bucketed by maturity and reset date); forward rate agreements and interest rate futures as a combination of short and long positions; options by delta times notional.

Hedging with a forward rate agreement (courseware annexure): a forward rate agreement (FRA) is an over-the-counter contract fixing the interest rate for a future period on a notional amount; it is cash settled on the difference between the contract rate and the floating reference rate; the notional is not exchanged. Scenario: a bank takes a foreign currency non-resident deposit of USD 1 million at 1.45 per cent for 3 years and deploys the funds in the interbank market at 1.50 per cent for one year: after one year the bank must reinvest for two years at an unknown rate, so it is exposed to a fall in rates (if rates fall below 1.45 per cent it makes a loss); the bank enters a 1/3 FRA, receiving fixed at 1.46 per cent and paying the reference rate plus a spread, so that if rates fall the FRA gain offsets the lower placement income and if rates rise the FRA loss is offset by higher placement income, leaving the net result at about USD 500 in the first year and USD 100 in each later year in both scenarios in the courseware tables. The principle: an FRA locks the reinvestment rate.

payload.title: Interest rate risk: why it matters and how it arises
payload.core_explanation_md:
Until about **1970** banks took deposits and lent at **regulated rates**, so rate risk was small. **Deregulation** left pricing to **commercial judgement**; many failures came from **long-term fixed rate assets funded by short-term volatile liabilities**.

**Interest rate risk** = how far a bank's financial condition is exposed to **adverse rate movements**. Some risk is a **normal source of profit**, but **excessive risk threatens earnings and capital**.

**Two effects:**

- **Earnings:** rates change **net interest income (NII)** and rate-sensitive fee income and costs.
- **Economic value:** **rising rates raise discount rates and cut market values**; holding **longer-maturity assets than liabilities** means asset values fall **more** than liability values when rates rise.

**NIM = NII / earning assets.** Rate risk arises because assets and liabilities differ in their **principal amounts, maturity dates or repricing dates**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: It is a normal risk of banking, which becomes dangerous only when unmanaged.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Net interest income divided by earning assets.

payload.title: Gap or mismatch risk: asset and liability sensitivity
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **gap** is the difference between assets and liabilities whose **rates are reset in a given period**.

**Example 1:** Rs 100 crore of **two-year assets at 10 per cent** funded by **one-year liabilities at 9 per cent**: year-one profit **1 per cent (Rs 1 crore)**; in year two the liabilities are **rolled over**: if the rate rises to **11 per cent**, the bank loses **1 per cent**.

**Example 2:**

- A **91-day 8 per cent deposit in a 91-day T-bill at 10 per cent**: no mismatch; **200 bp preserved**.
- The same deposit funding a **monthly-repriced floating loan** makes the bank **asset sensitive**: NII **rises if rates rise** and falls if they fall.
- The deposit funding a **5-year fixed rate mortgage** makes the bank **liability sensitive**: NII **falls if rates rise** and rises if they fall.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Whichever side reprices sooner decides who gains from a rate move.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a bank asset sensitive or liability sensitive if its deposits reprice before its fixed rate loans?

payload.title: Basis risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
Even with **matched repricing dates**, different instruments' rates **rarely move by the same amount**. **Basis risk** = the risk that **rates on different assets and liabilities change by different magnitudes**.

**Courseware example:** repricing assets: call money **50** and cash credit **40** (total 90); repricing liabilities: savings **50** and fixed deposits **50** (total 100): **negative gap 10**; a **1 per cent parallel fall** should improve NII by Rs 1 crore.

If rates actually fall **1.0 (call), 0.7 (cash credit), 0.5 (savings), 0.4 (fixed)**:

- Interest income falls **0.50 + 0.28 = 0.78**.
- Interest expense falls **0.25 + 0.20 = 0.45**.
- **NII falls by 0.78 - 0.45 = Rs 0.33 crore.**

Basis risk is high where **composite assets** are funded by **composite liabilities** and in **volatile** conditions.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A parallel shift is a simplification; real rates move by different amounts.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The risk that interest rates on different assets and liabilities change by different amounts.

payload.title: Net interest position, embedded option, yield curve, price and reinvestment risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Net interest position** | More **interest-earning assets** than **interest-bearing liabilities**: NII **falls as rates fall**, rises as they rise |
| **Embedded option** | **Prepayment of loans** or **early withdrawal of deposits**; borrowers **prepay when rates fall**, so the bank earns less (a 10 per cent loan funded at 8 per cent, prepaid after 30 days with rates at 9 per cent: spread **200 bp** for 30 days, **100 bp** after) |
| **Yield curve** | The **slope or shape** of the yield curve changes; if the curve **inverts**, NII can shrink (courseware: **250 bp falls to 100 bp**) |
| **Price** | **Selling before maturity**: bond **prices and yields move inversely**; linked to the **trading book** |
| **Reinvestment** | Uncertainty about the **rate for reinvesting future cash flows**; the bond pricing formula assumes coupons are reinvested at the **YTM** |

**Price and reinvestment risk partly offset:** when rates **rise**, the bond **price falls** but **reinvestment income rises**; short-term bonds have more reinvestment risk, long-term bonds more price risk. **Matching duration** (not maturity) reduces reinvestment risk.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Prepayment is a one-way bet for the borrower: it happens when it benefits the borrower.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do borrowers tend to prepay when rates fall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: They can refinance at lower rates, leaving the bank to reinvest at lower yields.

payload.title: Earnings and economic value perspectives
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Perspective | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| **Earnings** | Effect of rate changes on **reported (accrual) earnings**, mainly **NII**; wider view includes **non-interest income** (servicing and securitisation fees, processing fees), which can also be **rate sensitive** |
| **Economic value** | **Present value of expected asset cash flows minus present value of liability cash flows plus off-balance sheet flows**: the **net worth** sensitivity; a **fuller long-term view** than near-term earnings |

**Example:** a **5-year 10 per cent bond** when market rates rise to **12 per cent** falls in price (a Rs 100 bond may fetch around Rs 95 in the courseware illustration): a loss on marking to market.

**Embedded losses:** instruments **not marked to market** may already hold **gains or losses from past rate moves** that show up in earnings over time (a **long-term fixed rate loan** made when rates were low and **funded later at higher rates** drains resources for its life).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Near-term earnings can hide a large fall in economic value.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the economic value perspective measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The sensitivity of the present value of the bank net worth to changes in interest rates.

payload.title: Measuring interest rate risk: repricing schedule, gap and duration
payload.core_explanation_md:
A measurement system must **capture all material sources**, use **accepted techniques** and have **documented assumptions**.

**Repricing schedule:** put rate-sensitive assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet items into **time bands** by **maturity (fixed)** or **next repricing (floating)**; items without clear dates (**sight and savings deposits**, **prepayable mortgages**) are placed by **judgement and past behaviour**.

**Gap analysis:** **gap = RSA - RSL** per band; **change in NII ≈ gap x rate change**.

- **Negative (liability sensitive) gap:** a **rise** in rates **reduces** NII.
- **Positive (asset sensitive) gap:** a **fall** reduces NII.
- **Shortcomings:** ignores **differences within a band**, **basis risk**, **timing of payments**, **options**, and **non-interest income**; a **rough** approximation.

**Duration:** sensitivity weights by band estimate the **change in economic value**; limitations: mainly **repricing risk**, **average duration per band**, and weak on **options**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Gap analysis looks at earnings; duration looks at economic value.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank has a negative gap. What happens to NII if rates rise?

payload.title: Gap table: cumulative gap and NII effect
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Gap(band) = RSA - RSL.**

**Cumulative gap = sum of gaps up to the band.**

**Change in NII = cumulative gap x change in rate** (for the horizon the cumulative gap covers).

**Sensitivity ratio = RSA / RSL.**

Courseware table (Rs crore): 1 day **-50**; up to 3 months **-200** (cum **-250**); 3-6 months **-100** (**-350**); 6-12 months **-200** (**-550**); 1-3 years **-300** (**-850**); 3-5 years **+200** (**-650**); over 5 years **+650** (**0**). With a **cumulative one-year gap of -550**, a **1 per cent rise** cuts NII by **Rs 5.50 crore**.

variables.name: Cumulative repricing gap up to the horizon

assumptions: Gap measured to a one-year horizon
common_errors: Using the gap of one band only for the cumulative effect

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The result is an annualised approximation because bands reprice at different times.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the NII effect of a 1 per cent rise with a cumulative one-year gap of minus Rs 400 crore?

payload.title: Simulation approaches and difficult positions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Static simulation:** assesses cash flows from **current positions** under rate scenarios (**shifts or tilts** of the yield curve) and **discounts them** to estimate the change in economic value.

**Dynamic simulation:** adds assumptions about the **future course of rates** and **changes in business** (new loans, pricing strategy, customer behaviour); can capture **embedded options**; but must not become a **black box**.

**Difficult positions:** where **behavioural maturity differs from contractual maturity**:

- **Mortgages:** prepayments fall as rates rise, rise as rates fall.
- **Non-maturity deposits** (current and savings accounts): withdrawable at will and their rates **do not move closely** with market rates.

Banks use **past behaviour**, **statistical or econometric analysis** and **prepayment models**, and take **input from business units** about planned strategies.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The quality of the result depends on the quality of the behavioural assumptions.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between static and dynamic simulation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Static simulation uses current positions only; dynamic simulation adds assumptions about future rates and business activity.

payload.title: Modified duration gap and equity value sensitivity
payload.core_explanation_md:
**W = RSL / RSA.**

**DGAP = DA - W x DL**, where **DA** and **DL** are the weighted average **modified durations** of assets and liabilities.

**Leverage = RSA / equity.**

**Modified duration of equity = DGAP x leverage.**

**Change in equity value (%) = modified duration of equity x rate change (in per cent).**

Courseware illustration: **DA 1.96, DL 1.25, W 1.02**: **DGAP = 1.96 - 1.02 x 1.25 = 0.69**; **leverage 13.52**; **modified duration of equity 9.34**; for a **200 bp** shock the **equity value falls by 18.68 per cent** (9.34 x 2).

assumptions: Modified durations measured at the mid-point of each band
common_errors: Applying the rate change in basis points instead of per cent

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Leverage magnifies a small duration gap into a large change in the value of equity.

self_check.prompt_text: What does leverage do to the equity value sensitivity?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It multiplies the duration gap, so the equity value changes by more than the assets or liabilities.

payload.title: Strategies to control interest rate risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
The aim is to change the **interest rate sensitivity** of the balance sheet. A cautious bank **matches** assets and liabilities to bring the **gap towards zero**; an aggressive bank **varies the gap with its rate forecast** (expecting rates to rise, it **reprices assets more often than liabilities**).

| To reduce **asset sensitivity** | To reduce **liability sensitivity** |
| --- | --- |
| **Extend investment maturities** | **Shorten investment maturities** |
| **Increase floating rate deposits** | **Increase floating rate lending** |
| **Increase fixed rate lending** | **Increase long-term deposits** |
| **Sell floating rate loans** | **Increase short-term lending** |
| **Increase short-term borrowings** | |
| **Increase long-term lending** | |

**Other options:** fund long-term assets with **liabilities that bear no interest**; pair repriceable assets with repriceable liabilities; use **FRAs, swaps, options and futures** for **synthetic hedges**; keep **NPAs** low because they worsen maturity mismatch. A **full match is neither feasible nor prudent**: set **tolerance limits on gaps**, tighter for the **near buckets**, and build **in-house forecasting skill**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The lists are two sides of the same coin: one reduces asset sensitivity, the other liability sensitivity.

self_check.prompt_text: Give one action that reduces asset sensitivity.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example extending the maturity of the investment portfolio.

payload.title: Controls and sound practice in interest rate risk management
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Internal controls:** a **strong control environment** and compliance culture, an adequate process to **identify and evaluate risk**, **policies, procedures and methodologies**, **adequate information systems** and **continual review of adherence**. Reviews are done **regularly by people independent of the function**, and for complex exposures by an **independent party** (internal or external auditor or risk experts).

**Four elements of sound practice:**

1. **Board and senior management oversight.**
2. **Adequate risk management policies and procedures.**
3. **Appropriate risk measurement, monitoring and control functions.**
4. **Comprehensive internal controls and independent audits.**

- The **board** approves strategies and policies and is **regularly informed** of the exposure.
- **Senior management** keeps **limits**, **systems and standards** for measuring risk, valuing positions and performance, and **reporting**.
- **Separation of duties:** the **risk measurement, monitoring and control** function must be **independent** of position-taking.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Independence stops the people who take the risk from judging it.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four elements of sound interest rate risk management.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Board and senior management oversight, policies and procedures, measurement monitoring and control functions, and internal controls and independent audits.

payload.title: Interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB): principles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**IRRBB** = the current or prospective risk to a bank's **capital and earnings** from adverse rate moves that affect **banking book** positions: changes in rates change the **present value and timing of cash flows**, hence **economic value**, and affect **NII**.

- The ALM guidelines **bucket** positions by **rate sensitivity**; for **non-maturity deposits** banks estimate **behavioural patterns** and place them in buckets; banks that cannot use the **standardised approach**.
- **Capital** for rate risk in **trading book** positions is added to RWA; under **Pillar 2** banks assess **banking book** rate risk from **short and long-term** perspectives. The central bank does not permit trading in **banking book** securities.

**Enhanced guidelines (principles):**

- **Governance:** **Board-approved IRRBB risk appetite statement**, **regular monitoring**, **procedures to approve major hedging or risk-taking**, **escalation of violations** of limits, and **identification of IRRBB in all products**.
- **Measurement:** compute IRRBB from **earnings and economic value** perspectives using **internal shock scenarios**, **historical and hypothetical stress scenarios** and **prescribed scenarios**.

Dates, scenario counts and thresholds are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: IRRBB is about the long-held banking book, not the trading book.

self_check.prompt_text: Which book is IRRBB concerned with?

payload.title: Hedging reinvestment risk with a forward rate agreement
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **FRA** is an **OTC contract** fixing the interest rate for a **future period** on a **notional** amount; it is **cash settled** on the difference between the **contract rate** and the **reference rate**; **the notional is not exchanged**.

**Scenario:** a bank accepts a **3-year FCNR deposit** of USD 1 million at **1.45 per cent** and places the funds in the interbank market for **one year at 1.50 per cent**. After a year it must **reinvest for two years at an unknown rate**. If rates **fall below 1.45 per cent** it loses.

**Hedge:** a **1/3 FRA** in which the bank **receives fixed** (1.46 per cent) and pays the reference rate plus a spread locks in the rate. If rates **fall**, the **FRA gain offsets** the lower placement income; if rates **rise**, the **FRA loss is offset** by higher placement income. The net result is stable in both cases: **an FRA locks the reinvestment rate.**

unresolved: The courseware sections on the central bank guidelines on interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB: Board-approved limits, standard stress tests, the six prescribed shock scenarios, the Basel standards of April 2016, draft guidelines circulated in February 2017 and implementation from April 2019) are dated and were not checked against primary sources; they are taught only as principles (governance, measurement from earnings and economic value perspectives) and not as current rules. The detailed IRRBB standardised framework is not taught.

The courseware worked examples were recomputed and agree: the basis risk statement (call money 50 and cash credit 40 against savings 50 and fixed deposits 50; loss in NII of Rs 0.33 crore), the yield curve example (NII 250 bp falling to 100 bp), the cumulative one-year gap of Rs 550 crore with a 1 per cent rate rise reducing NII by Rs 5.50 crore, the economic value of equity illustration (modified duration of equity 9.34, 200 bp shock giving an equity value drop of 18.68 per cent), the bond price illustration (a 10 per cent bond repriced when yields rise to 12 per cent falling to about Rs 95 for a 5-year bond: the true price at 12 per cent for a 5-year 10 per cent annual coupon bond is Rs 92.79, so the courseware Rs 95 figure is an approximation, not taught as exact).
The courseware states that the earlier "3-6-3" banking rule and that rules governing banks before 1970 prevented interest rate risk; these are narrative history, not taught as fact.

The courseware FRA annexure example (FCNR deposit USD 1 million at 1.45 per cent for three years funded in the interbank market at 1.50 per cent for one year, with a 1/3 FRA) is a worked illustration using small interest rates; its cash flow tables are partly rounded. The principle (an FRA locks the reinvestment rate) is taught and items use new figures.

The courseware text on Economic Value Added (EVA) in the economic value perspective cites an academic definition and lists advantages and disadvantages that concern corporate EVA, not the bank economic value of equity; it is not taught here.

The courseware advises banks to reduce asset sensitivity by extending investment maturities and increasing floating rate deposits and so on; it is taught as the courseware list of strategies for the case of a bank that is asset sensitive and expects rates to fall, with the reverse list for liability sensitivity.
Numbers in the numerical items are invented and checked in tests/content/batch-bfm-d-u05-b001.test.ts.
The courseware check-your-progress questions were not copied; questions are independently written.
